Case Study: Furniture Workshop

Read the passage carefully, then answer the 5 MCQs in the test below.

A small furniture workshop in Jodhpur makes two products for a hotel order: wooden bookshelves and cabinets. Each bookshelf takes 3 hours of carpentry and 1 hour of finishing, while each cabinet takes 2 hours of carpentry and 2 hours of finishing. In a working week the single carpenter is available for 36 hours and the finishing bench for 24 hours; neither can be exceeded. The owner earns a profit of ₹ 200 on every bookshelf and ₹ 160 on every cabinet sold, and wants to plan the week's output to make the profit as large as possible. Before drawing any graph she writes the problem as a linear programming model, letting x stand for the number of bookshelves and y for the number of cabinets built that week, then sketches the feasible region shown.

questions.q: The objective function the owner wants to maximise is
questions.explanation: Profit is ₹ 200 per bookshelf (x) and ₹ 160 per cabinet (y), to be made as large as possible: Maximise Z=200x+160y. (a).
Carpentry uses 3 h per bookshelf and 2 h per cabinet, capped at 36 h: 3x+2y≤ 36. (c).
Finishing uses 1 h per bookshelf and 2 h per cabinet, capped at 24 h: x+2y≤ 24. (b).

questions.q: Together with the resource limits, the model must also include
questions.explanation: Counts of items cannot be negative, so the non-negativity restrictions x≥ 0,\ y≥ 0 must be added. (d).

questions.q: Is the plan (x,y)=(8,6) feasible for this workshop?
questions.explanation: Carpentry: 3(8)+2(6)=36≤ 36; finishing: 8+2(6)=20≤ 24; both ≥ 0. All constraints hold, so (8,6) is feasible. (a).
